summary: Specifies a binding from iTIP, the calendar scheduling protocol, to email transports. iCalendar entries are wrapped in RFC 5322 messages and MIME so meeting invitations and replies can be exchanged by email.

plainLanguage.summary:
An iCalendar object is the structured text that describes a meeting: who is organising it, who is invited, when it starts and what it is called. This RFC says how to put that text inside an email.

The object goes into a part of the message marked as text/calendar, with a parameter saying whether it is a request or a reply. A receiving program reads that part, works out who really sent it by checking the S/MIME signature, and then checks that sender is allowed to make the change they asked for.

questions: how do calendar invitations work over email
how are calendar invitations sent by email
what is the text/calendar media type
subtitle: How calendar invitations and replies travel inside ordinary MIME email messages.

tldr.problem: The calendaring protocol iTIP says what to send to arrange a meeting, but not how to carry it over the network. Email is the transport almost everyone already has.
tldr.mechanism: iMIP wraps an iCalendar object in a MIME body part with the content type text/calendar, adds the method parameter so the receiver knows whether it is a request or a reply, and sends it over SMTP. It also says how to sign and encrypt those body parts so the sender can be checked.
tldr.outcome: Meeting invitations, replies and cancellations can travel as ordinary email that a person can also read in plain text. This RFC obsoletes RFC 2447.

today: RFC 6047 is a Proposed Standard from December 2010. It obsoletes RFC 2447 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The "text/calendar" media type was registered in RFC 5545.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document provides the transport-specific information, called a binding, necessary to convey the iCalendar Transport-independent Interoperability Protocol (iTIP) over Internet email using MIME. It therefore defines the iCalendar Message-Based Interoperability Protocol (iMIP).

Implementers need to be familiar with several other memos that, along with this one, form the framework for Internet calendaring and scheduling standards. RFC 5545 specifies the core objects, data types, properties and property parameters of iCalendar. RFC 5546 specifies the interoperability protocol for scheduling between different implementations. This memo does not repeat those concepts; where possible it refers to the memo that defines them.

The memo also sets out the formatting conventions it uses. Calendaring and scheduling roles are written in quoted text with each word capitalised, so "Organizer" is a role of a "Calendar User". Calendar components are written in capitalised quoted text and all start with the letter "V", so "VEVENT" is the event component, "VTODO" the to-do component and "VJOURNAL" the journal component. Scheduling methods are written the same way, so "REQUEST" asks for a component to be created or modified and "REPLY" is how a recipient tells the "Organizer" their status.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is one piece of a set. One memo defines what a calendar entry looks like, another defines the conversation between two calendars, and this one defines the envelope: how that conversation is carried by email.

sections.title: How a Scheduling Message Travels by Email
sections.content:
The section refers to the "originator" and the "recipient" of an iMIP message. In the case of a request method the originator is the "Organizer" and the recipient is an "Attendee" of the event. In the case of a response method the originator is an "Attendee" and the recipient is the "Organizer".

The RFC 5322 "Reply-To" header field typically contains the email address of the originator of the scheduling message, but this cannot be guaranteed: the sender of the iMIP message might not be the originator, and the sender's mail user agent might not enforce iMIP semantics by translating the originator's address into the "Reply-To" field.

The calendar address given in the "ORGANIZER" and "ATTENDEE" properties must be a proper "mailto:" URI for the corresponding "Organizer" or "Attendee". Because iTIP does not stop "Attendees" from forwarding events or to-dos, the RFC 5322 "Sender" value may not equal that of the "Organizer", and the "Organizer" or "Attendee" cannot be reliably inferred from the "Sender" or "Reply-To" header fields. The relevant address must be ascertained by opening the "text/calendar" body part and examining the "ATTENDEE" and "ORGANIZER" properties.
sections.plainLanguage: A meeting invitation goes from the person organising the meeting to the people invited. The reply goes back the other way. Because an invitation can be forwarded, the program cannot trust the email headers to say who really sent it; it has to look inside the calendar part.

sections.title: The Content-Type Header Field
sections.content:
A MIME body part containing content information that conforms to this document must have a "Content-Type" value of "text/calendar". The header field must also include the MIME parameter "method", whose value must be the same, ignoring case, as the value of the "METHOD" property within the iCalendar object.

A MIME message containing multiple iCalendar objects with different "method" values must be further encapsulated with a "multipart/mixed" MIME entity, so that each iCalendar object sits in its own "text/calendar" entity. A body part with a "Content-Type" value of "text/calendar" that lacks the "method" parameter is not considered to be an iMIP body part and is not subject to the requirements of this document.

The default character set for iCalendar objects is UTF-8, but the default character set for a "text/*" MIME entity is US-ASCII. A "charset" MIME parameter must therefore be present if the iCalendar object contains characters that cannot be represented in US-ASCII, and it must have the value "UTF-8". The optional "component" MIME parameter defines the iCalendar component type contained within the object. A typical header looks like this: Content-Type: text/calendar; method=REQUEST; charset=UTF-8; component=vevent.

The "text/calendar" content type allows the scheduling message to be included in a MIME message with other content information, that is a "multipart/mixed" message, or with a clear-text, human-readable form of the scheduling message, that is a "multipart/alternative" message. So that people using mail programs that do not support "text/calendar" can still read the message, scheduling messages should be sent with an alternative, human-readable form. "multipart/alternative" must not be used to represent two slightly different iCalendar objects, for example two "VEVENT"s with alternative starting times.

Any receiving user agent compliant with this specification must be able to process "text/calendar" body parts enclosed within a "multipart/*" entity, and a "multipart/mixed" message can include multiple "text/calendar" components, all of which it must be able to process.
sections.plainLanguage: The calendar part of the email says what it is in three words: the type is text/calendar, the method says request or reply, and the charset says how the text is encoded. An optional fourth word says which kind of entry it is, such as an event.

sections.title: Transfer Encoding and Content Disposition
sections.content:
Unless an iMIP message is transported over an 8-bit clean transport such as SMTP with 8BITMIME, a transfer encoding such as quoted-printable or base64 must be used for iCalendar objects containing any characters that cannot be represented in the US-ASCII character set.

Implementations may include a "Content-Disposition" header field to define a file name for an iCalendar object. However, the handling of a MIME part must be based on its "Content-Type" and not on the extension given in "Content-Disposition", because email malware is known to trick user agents into misinterpreting the content of messages by specifying a file extension there that does not correspond to the value of the "Content-Type" header field.

The examples in the RFC show several shapes of message. A single component with an ATTACH property refers to an attachment by its URL. A client can emit a "multipart/alternative" message that includes both a plain text version and the full iCalendar object, so that clients which do not support "text/calendar" can still render the plain text representation. A message with an inline attachment refers to the attachment using a Content-ID, packaging the iCalendar object and the document in a "multipart/related" encapsulation.
sections.plainLanguage: Calendar text is usually plain ASCII, so it can travel as it is. If it contains other characters, it has to be encoded the way email normally encodes text. The name of an attached file must not decide how the part is handled; the content type must.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security threats that applications must address when implementing iTIP are detailed in RFC 5546. In particular, two spoofing threats are identified there: spoofing the "Organizer" and spoofing an "Attendee". To address them, the originator of an iCalendar object must be authenticated by a recipient. Compliant applications must support signing and encrypting "text/calendar" body parts using a mechanism based on S/MIME.

The steps for processing a signed iMIP message are these. First, use S/MIME to determine who signed the "text/calendar" body part; this is the signer, whose email address must be given in the rfc822Name field of the subject alternative name extension of the signer certificate. The signer is not necessarily the person who sent the email, since a message can be forwarded. Second, correlate the signer to an "ATTENDEE" property or to the "ORGANIZER" property, based on the method and the calendar component. If the signer cannot be correlated, warn the user that the object is untrusted and encourage them to ignore the message, while still giving advanced users the option to view the certificate and chain and then accept the object. Third, determine whether that "ATTENDEE" or "ORGANIZER" is authorized to perform the operation; if the conditions are not met, ignore the message. Fourth, if all the conditions are met, the message can be processed.

Only the "Organizer" is authorized to modify or cancel entries she organizes, and only the respondent has the authorization to indicate their status to the "Organizer". Authentication must be performed using S/MIME, and unauthenticated messages may not be trusted.

If an unsigned iMIP message is received from a sender who previously sent signed messages, the receiving program should warn the user about a possible man-in-the-middle attack and ignore the message unless the user overrides this. iMIP does not restrict a calendar user agent from forwarding iCalendar objects to other users or agents, and there is no mechanism to verify whether a "Calendar User" has authorised someone to work on their behalf through the "sent-by" parameter, so implementations must provide a way for users to make that decision: by rejecting messages from anyone other than the "ORGANIZER" or the "ATTENDEE"s, by keeping a list of trusted proxies in local security policy, or by prompting the user.
sections.plainLanguage: Because an invitation can be forwarded or forged, the receiving program checks four things in order: who signed the calendar part, whether that signer is named in the invitation, whether that person is allowed to make this change, and only then processes it. If the signer is not named in the invitation, the user is warned.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives a minimal message showing how an iCalendar object references an attachment that is accessible by its URL, with a "Content-Type" of "text/calendar; method=REQUEST; charset=US-ASCII" and a 7-bit content transfer encoding.

It also shows a message that uses "multipart/alternative" for low-fidelity clients, with a plain text part and a "text/calendar" part in the same message, and a message with an inline attachment, in which the iCalendar object refers to the attached document with a Content-ID and the two are packaged in a "multipart/related" encapsulation. Further examples cover multiple similar components, multiple mixed components, and detailed components with an ATTACH property.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the shapes a message can take: a plain invitation, an invitation with a readable summary for people whose software cannot read the calendar, and an invitation with a document attached.

sections.title: Recommended Practices
sections.content:
The iCalendar specification makes frequent use of URIs for data types in properties such as "DESCRIPTION", "ATTACH" and "CONTACT". Two forms of URIs are the Message ID and the Content-ID, both defined in RFC 2392.

Although RFC 2392 allows referencing messages or MIME body parts in other MIME entities or stores, it is strongly recommended that iMIP implementations include all referenced messages and body parts in a single MIME entity. If an iCalendar object contains Content-ID or Message-ID references to other messages or body parts, implementations should ensure that these are transmitted with the iCalendar object. If they are not, there is no guarantee that the receiving calendar user agent will have the access or the authorization to view those objects.
sections.plainLanguage: If the invitation points at another file or another message, send that file along with the invitation. If it is left behind, the program receiving the invitation may not be allowed to fetch it.

messages.label: REQUEST
messages.note: The organizer sends a scheduling message. The iCalendar object is wrapped in a text/calendar body part whose method parameter is REQUEST.

messages.note: The attendee replies with their status. The reply is wrapped in the same way, with a method parameter of REPLY.

viz.caption: A minimal iMIP message, from the examples in the RFC

data.title: A request for a meeting
data.code:
From: sman@netscape.example.com
To: stevesil@microsoft.example.com
Subject: Phone Conference
Mime-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: text/calendar; method=REQUEST; charset=US-ASCII
Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit

BEGIN:VCALENDAR
PRODID:-//Example/ExampleCalendarClient//EN
METHOD:REQUEST
VERSION:2.0
BEGIN:VEVENT
ORGANIZER:mailto:man@netscape.example.com
ATTENDEE;ROLE=CHAIR;PARTSTAT=ACCEPTED:mailto:man@netscape.example.com
ATTENDEE;RSVP=YES:mailto:stevesil@microsoft.example.com
DTSTAMP:19970611T190000Z
DTSTART:19970701T210000Z
DTEND:19970701T230000Z
SUMMARY:Phone Conference
DESCRIPTION:Please review the attached document.
UID:calsvr.example.com-873970198738777
ATTACH:ftp://ftp.bar.example.com/pub/docs/foo.doc
STATUS:CONFIRMED
END:VEVENT
END:VCALENDAR

viz.caption: The four steps for checking a signed scheduling message

items.title: 1. Find the signer
items.text: Use S/MIME to find who signed the text/calendar part. The signer is not necessarily the person who sent the email.

items.title: 2. Match the signer
items.text: Correlate the signer with an ATTENDEE or ORGANIZER property. If there is no match, warn the user and treat the object as untrusted.

items.title: 3. Check authorisation
items.text: Decide whether that ATTENDEE or ORGANIZER may perform this operation. If not, ignore the message.

items.title: 4. Process the message
items.text: If every condition is met, the message can be processed.
